title: Watch These Orcas Smash a Giant Dead Fish to Pieces-Just for Kicks
text:
The ramming behavior might help younger orcas more easily digest their food, while also allowing other orcas to have a little fun, researchers say.
The ramming behavior might help younger orcas more easily digest their food, while also allowing other orcas to have a little fun, researchers say. Despite living their entire lives in the water, killer whales share a lot in common with humans.
Research out today shows that some can pull off the sort of antics you’d expect to see on an episode of) ramming into an already dead fish and blowing it into pieces. The mysterious behavior may be a sign of parental assistance among these killer whales or an example of these creatures having a good time.
“We propose that this ‘ram-to-fragment’ behavior may have multiple functions, including facilitating foraging for juvenile orcas or reflecting play behavior,” the researchers wrote in their paper,Despite the nickname, orcas are actually a type of dolphin, though dolphins and whales are part of the same broad order of marine mammals called cetaceans. , weren’t looking to discover a new kind of orca hijinks.
They were observing a pod of orcas in the Gulf of California that had killed a sharp-tailed sunfish . Sunfish are one of the largest and heaviest groups of bony fish, with some members extending up to 11 feet long and weighing up to 4,400 pounds. The team recorded one female orca holding onto the sunfish by its tail fin as another male rushed toward the two.
The female then let go of the sunfish just before the male collided into it, causing the corpse to burst open like a flesh piñata. More than a year later, in September 2025, a third party caught a similar event on camera in the Gulf of California, once again featuring one killer whale holding onto a sunfish while another rammed into it. The repeated and coordinated movement of these whales strongly suggests it’s an intentional behavior, the researchers say.
Yet there are still many questions about its nature. Orcas can’t chew their food, so for larger prey they’ll tear away chunks that are then swallowed whole. The killer whales’ ramming might be used to break the sunfish into more digestible pieces for the youngest members of the pod, akin to a parent cutting up a steak for their child.
Orcas have beenusing complex group movements to rip apart their prey, then sharing those chunks with the rest of the pod . Notably, in the July 2024 event, a juvenile whale in the group ate some of the smaller sunfish pieces that flew off post-ramming, while the adults ate from the largest remnant of the body that stayed intact.
That said, it’s possible this behavior may instead or also be an instance of these orcas literally playing with their food. Orcas have observed doing other strange things with their prey, likesea lions up in the air or swatting stingrays around like a soccer ball. Though these tricks can help them successfully catch their prey without injury, sometimes they’ll do it without eventheir kill.
Some scientists theorize this play behavior is used to help younger orcas learn how to hunt or simply to bond socially. And there may yet be other explanations for the orca ramming. Much like humans, different populations and individual pods of cetaceans can have substantial differences from one another in how they behave and communicate. These differences are passed down socially, similar to how humans teach their young long-lasting traditions and languages.
So another interesting question is how extensive this ramming behavior might be among orcas living in the Gulf of California or elsewhere, and if it only applies to this particular species of prey. Unfortunately, the researchers weren’t able to tell whether the same pod was involved in both events they documented. Whatever the explanation, it’s clear there’s still plenty we don’t know about killer whales, the researchers say—mysteries that will take better data to solve.
“This emphasizes the importance of obtaining high-quality dorsal fin and eye patch imagery to enable individual and pod identification and to better characterize feeding behavior,” the researchers wrote. “Continued photo-identification efforts in the Mexican Pacific and Gulf of California will help clarify the degree of dietary specialization among pods. ” In any case, it’s comforting to know that humans aren’t the only animals to occasionally be weird with their food.
And now I’m wondering if orcas have ever tried to mimic a walrus with the ocean version of French fries.
